---
title: "How is it cut out and put together?"
---

{{< include _model.qmd >}}

Every part flattened from the model's own tables and nested on one sheet, then
written out at 1:1. The outlines are generated here rather than drawn, so the
template cannot drift from the aircraft the rest of the chapter analyses.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Specified
**Sheet: A3, 27 g** · from the original brief · it sets both the mass and the
space available, so it decides the nesting.

**Output: a scale layout plus a true 1:1 PDF** · asked of the user, 2026-08-30 ·
the PDF is the usable artefact; the figure is what makes the entry readable.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Assumed
The two fuselage laminations are spliced at different stations so the butt
joints are bridged by continuous material in the other layer. The original plan
interlocks a single pair of pieces with zigzag teeth instead; staggering is
simpler to cut and stronger in a laminate. Cut lines are the finished outline —
no allowance is added for the knife.
:::

```{python}
MM, A3 = 1e3, (420.0, 297.0)             # mm, the specified sheet, landscape
SPLIT_A, SPLIT_B = 0.2665, 0.1800        # m, staggered splice stations

parts = {
    "wing": sym_surface(wing_eta, wing_c, b_w / 2),
    "stabilizer": sym_surface(stab_eta, stab_c, b_h / 2),
    "fin": fin_outline(),
    "fuselage A, nose": fuselage_outline(0, SPLIT_A),
    "fuselage A, tail": fuselage_outline(SPLIT_A, l_fus),
    "fuselage B, nose": fuselage_outline(0, SPLIT_B),
    "fuselage B, tail": fuselage_outline(SPLIT_B, l_fus),
}
# nest() raises if anything falls off the sheet or two parts overlap, so a bad
# template stops the render rather than reaching the printer.
placed = nest(parts, {
    "wing": (10, 8), "fin": (320, 8), "stabilizer": (10, 113),
    "fuselage B, tail": (160, 113), "fuselage A, nose": (10, 184),
    "fuselage B, nose": (10, 228), "fuselage A, tail": (200, 228),
}, A3)

foam = S_w + S_h + S_v + 2 * S_fus
PDF = "chapters/02-mceagle-300/mceagle-300-cutting-plan-a3.pdf"
```

**Answer.** All seven pieces fit one A3 sheet, using
`{python} f"{foam/(A3[0]*A3[1]/MM**2)*100:.0f}"`% of its area and
`{python} f"{foam*sigma*1e3:.2f}"` g of its `{python} f"{A3[0]*A3[1]/MM**2*sigma*1e3:.1f}"` g —
so one sheet builds the glider with more than half left over.

The fuselage is the constraint. At `{python} f"{l_fus*MM:.1f}"` mm it overhangs
A3's `{python} f"{A3[0]:.0f}"` mm edge by
`{python} f"{(l_fus*MM - A3[0]):.1f}"` mm, so it cannot be cut in one piece —
which is precisely why the original plan splits its fuselage and interlocks the
halves. The same constraint reappears at this scale. Here it is cut as two
laminations spliced `{python} f"{abs(SPLIT_A-SPLIT_B)*MM:.0f}"` mm apart, so
each butt joint is backed by unbroken foam in the other layer.

[**Download the 1:1 cutting plan (A3 PDF)**](mceagle-300-cutting-plan-a3.pdf) —
print at 100%, not "fit to page", and check the printed wing measures
`{python} f"{b_w*MM:.0f}"` mm tip to tip before cutting anything.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cutting
#| fig-cap: "The seven parts nested on one A3 sheet. Drawn from the model's own chord tables and depth profile, and written out at 1:1 as the linked PDF."
def draw(ax):
    for n, p in placed.items():
        ax.fill(p[:, 0], p[:, 1], facecolor="none", edgecolor="k", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xlim(0, A3[0]); ax.set_ylim(0, A3[1])
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")


# The 1:1 artefact: an A3 page with one drawing unit to the millimetre.
pdf = plt.figure(figsize=(A3[0] / 25.4, A3[1] / 25.4))
draw(pdf.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1]))
pdf.savefig(PDF); plt.close(pdf)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.7))
draw(ax)
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, 0), *A3, fill=False, ec="0.6", lw=1))
for n, p in placed.items():
    ax.text(p[:, 0].mean(), p[:, 1].mean(), n, ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=6.5, color="0.45")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-build
#| tbl-cap: "Where each part goes, measured from the nose along the fuselage's straight top edge."
import pandas as pd

x_np = neutral_point()
m_b = ballast_for(x_np - 0.10 * c_w, 0.0)
mp = mass_properties(m_ballast=m_b, x_ballast=0.0)

pd.DataFrame({
    "step": ["laminate the fuselage", "wing leading edge", "wing dihedral",
             "stabilizer trailing edge", "stabilizer incidence",
             "fin trailing edge", "nose ballast", "check: balance point"],
    "where / how much": [
        f"2 layers, splices {abs(SPLIT_A-SPLIT_B)*MM:.0f} mm apart",
        f"{x_le_w*MM:.1f} mm aft of the nose",
        f"tips {z_tip*MM:.1f} mm above the centre ({dihedral:.1f}°)",
        f"{x_te_v*MM:.1f} mm — flush with the tail, underneath",
        f"{i_h:.0f}° (trailing edge up)",
        f"{x_te_v*MM:.1f} mm — flush with the tail, on top",
        f"{m_b*1e3:.2f} g at the nose",
        f"{mp.x_cg*MM:.1f} mm aft of the nose",
    ],
}).style.hide(axis="index")
```

**Assembly.** Cut all seven pieces, marking the forward direction on each.
Laminate the two fuselage layers face to face with the splices offset, and let
them dry flat under a weight. Glue the stabilizer under the tail and the fin on
top of it, both trailing edges flush with the square end, and set the stabilizer
`{python} f"{abs(i_h):.0f}"`° trailing-edge-up relative to the wing — that
negative incidence is what lifts the nose out of a stall.

Divide the wing along its centreline, sand about 10 mm of each cut edge to a
`{python} f"{dihedral:.1f}"`° bevel, and glue the halves back together on top of
the fuselage with the leading edge `{python} f"{x_le_w*MM:.1f}"` mm aft of the
nose, propping the tips `{python} f"{z_tip*MM:.1f}"` mm up while it dries. The
finished wing spans `{python} f"{b_proj*MM:.0f}"` mm across the tips even though
`{python} f"{b_w*MM:.0f}"` mm of foam went into it — the dihedral takes the
difference.

Finally add `{python} f"{m_b*1e3:.2f}"` g at the nose and check it balances
`{python} f"{mp.x_cg*MM:.1f}"` mm back. Balance is the one thing worth measuring
rather than trusting: everything else tolerates a millimetre, and this does not.
